planting.note: Set out bare-root or containerized trees in January-February while dormant; needs only about 300-400 chill hours, so it fruits reliably across south Louisiana and coastal zone 8b-9a where higher-chill peaches fail.

directions: An LSU AgCenter release bred specifically for the low-chill winters of the Gulf South, producing heavy crops of medium-to-large, red-fuzzed, semi-freestone fruit with sweet golden flesh flecked red, ripening in mid-to-late June. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and prune to an open-center vase shape to let light into the canopy and reduce brown rot pressure in humid conditions. Thin fruit to about 6 inches apart in April to improve size, and watch for bacterial leaf spot and peach tree borer, both common on Gulf Coast stone fruit.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root stock in January-February; requires roughly 450 chill hours, placing it among the more reliable freestone options for south Louisiana and the wider northern Gulf Coast.

directions: Another LSU-bred freestone peach recommended for south Louisiana home orchards, ripening in late June with large yellow fruit streaked red and vigorous, productive trees. It pairs well with earlier-ripening La Peche to extend the harvest window on a small Gulf Coast home orchard. Site trees in full sun with excellent drainage, since peach roots are highly intolerant of standing water common after Gulf Coast summer downpours, and maintain a regular fungicide schedule to manage brown rot and scab in humid weather.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized trees in midwinter; this University of Florida release needs under 100 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any peach, so it sets fruit reliably even in mild coastal zone 9a-9b winters.

directions: Bred by the University of Florida stone fruit program for the state's subtropical climate, this very-low-chill freestone peach produces medium red-skinned fruit with soft, melting yellow flesh and good flavor for such an early-ripening variety. Because it blooms extremely early, protect flowers from occasional cold snaps and avoid planting in low-lying frost pockets. Keep trees pruned to an open, low-vase form for easy harvest and better airflow, which helps limit fungal disease in humid Gulf Coast springs.

planting.note: Plant while dormant in January-February; needs about 150 chill hours, well suited to north and central Florida, coastal Alabama, and other mild-winter Gulf Coast sites.

directions: An early University of Florida low-chill introduction bearing firm, juicy yellow-fleshed fruit with an attractive light red blush and a fairly long shelf life for a low-chill peach. It ripens earlier than most standard peaches, giving Gulf Coast gardeners fresh fruit well ahead of the general peach season. Grow in full sun with well-drained, slightly acidic soil, thin heavy fruit set for larger peaches, and monitor for bacterial spot, which can be more troublesome on early-blooming, low-chill types in wet springs.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; needs roughly 500-600 chill hours, so it performs best in the cooler-winter parts of zone 8-9 Gulf South rather than immediate mild-winter coastline.

directions: A California-bred medium-chill nectarine long grown across the Deep South for its large, semi-freestone fruit with olive-green skin blushed deep red and richly flavored yellow flesh, ripening in early-to-mid June. It sets fruit heavily and shows good tolerance to bacterial spot, but nectarines as a group are more prone to brown rot than peaches in humid Gulf climates, so maintain a preventive fungicide program through ripening. Choose an inland or upland Gulf South planting site over the immediate coast to ensure it receives adequate winter chilling for consistent bloom and fruit set.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in midwinter; needs about 750 chill hours, so it is best matched to the cooler-winter, upper Gulf South (inland zone 8) rather than the immediate mild coastline.

directions: An early-season Southern peach named for the 1976 US bicentennial, producing attractive medium-to-large freestone fruit with yellow flesh streaked red and good eating quality for an early ripener. It is a solid choice for growers in the cooler, higher-chill pockets of the Deep South who still want an early harvest, complementing very-low-chill coastal types on properties that span a range of microclimates. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, prune annually to an open-center form, and thin fruit in spring to improve size and reduce limb breakage from heavy crop loads.
